questions.stem: According to the Brønsted-Lowry model, an acid is a substance that:
options: accepts a pair of electrons from a base
donates a proton to another species
accepts a proton from another species
produces hydroxide ions in water
questions.explanation: In the Brønsted-Lowry model an acid is a proton (H⁺) donor and a base is a proton acceptor. Producing hydroxide ions in water is the Arrhenius definition of a base.

questions.stem: Which reaction is an acid-base reaction under the Brønsted-Lowry model but cannot be described as one by the Arrhenius model?
options: NH₃(g) + HCl(g) → NH₄Cl(s)
HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂SO₄(aq) + 2KOH(aq) → K₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
HNO₃(aq) + LiOH(aq) → LiNO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
questions.explanation: The Arrhenius model only covers acids and bases in aqueous solution, producing H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. In the gas-phase reaction HCl donates a proton to NH₃, so it is a Brønsted-Lowry acid-base reaction even though no water or hydroxide is involved.

questions.stem: Davy proposed an early model of acids. According to Davy, an acid is a substance that:
options: contains oxygen combined with a non-metal such as sulfur or carbon
produces hydroxide ions when it dissolves in water to form a solution
accepts a proton from a base when the two react in aqueous solution
contains hydrogen that can be partly or totally replaced by a metal
questions.explanation: Davy showed that acids such as hydrochloric acid contain no oxygen, and proposed that acids contain replaceable hydrogen. The idea that acids contain oxygen was the earlier model he challenged.

questions.stem: A solution of sodium carbonate is basic, even though Na₂CO₃ contains no hydroxide ions. How does the Brønsted-Lowry model explain this?
options: CO₃²⁻ ions donate protons to water molecules, producing H₃O⁺ ions
Na₂CO₃ dissociates to release hydroxide ions from the carbonate
CO₃²⁻ ions accept protons from water molecules, producing OH⁻ ions
Na⁺ ions accept protons from water molecules, producing OH⁻ ions
questions.explanation: Carbonate is a base: CO₃²⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻. The Arrhenius model, which needs a substance to release OH⁻ of its own, cannot explain this. Sodium ions do not react with water to any appreciable extent.

questions.stem: What is the conjugate base of H₂SO₄?
options: SO₃²⁻
HSO₄⁻
SO₄²⁻
H₃SO₄⁺
questions.explanation: A conjugate base has one proton fewer than its acid, so H₂SO₄ becomes HSO₄⁻. Sulfate, SO₄²⁻, is the conjugate base of HSO₄⁻, two protons away from H₂SO₄.

questions.stem: What is the conjugate acid of ammonia, NH₃?
options: H₃O⁺
OH⁻
NH₄⁺
NH₂⁻
questions.explanation: A conjugate acid has one more proton than its base, so NH₃ becomes NH₄⁺. Removing a proton instead gives NH₂⁻, the conjugate base.

questions.stem: In the reaction HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + OH⁻(aq), which are the two conjugate acid-base pairs?
options: HCO₃⁻ and H₂O; H₂CO₃ and OH⁻
HCO₃⁻ and OH⁻; H₂O and H₂CO₃
H₂CO₃ and H₂O; HCO₃⁻ and OH⁻
H₂CO₃ and HCO₃⁻; H₂O and OH⁻
questions.explanation: Each conjugate pair differs by one proton. HCO₃⁻ accepts a proton to become H₂CO₃, and H₂O donates a proton to become OH⁻. Reactant-with-reactant pairings are not conjugate pairs.

questions.stem: Which of these species can act as either a Brønsted-Lowry acid or a Brønsted-Lowry base?
options: NH₄⁺
Cl⁻
HCO₃⁻
CO₃²⁻
questions.explanation: An amphiprotic species can both donate and accept a proton. HCO₃⁻ can lose a proton to form CO₃²⁻ or gain one to form H₂CO₃. Carbonate has no proton to donate, and NH₄⁺ cannot accept another proton.

questions.stem: In which reaction does water act as a Brønsted-Lowry base?
options: CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COOH(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
HCl(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
questions.explanation: Water accepts a proton from HCl to form H₃O⁺, so it acts as a base. In the other three, water donates a proton and becomes OH⁻, so it acts as an acid.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the hydrogensulfate ion acting as a Brønsted-Lowry acid?
options: HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ H₂SO₄(aq) + H₂O(l)
SO₄²⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ SO₄²⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
HSO₄⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂SO₄(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
questions.explanation: As an acid, HSO₄⁻ donates its proton and becomes SO₄²⁻. In the second and third equations HSO₄⁻ gains a proton, acting as a base, and in the last it is the product, formed when sulfate acts as a base.

questions.stem: Which of these is a diprotic acid?
options: H₃PO₄
H₂SO₄
HCl
CH₃COOH
questions.explanation: Sulfuric acid can donate two protons per molecule. Ethanoic acid has four hydrogen atoms but only one is ionisable, so it is monoprotic, and phosphoric acid is triprotic.

questions.stem: Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, has four hydrogen atoms in each molecule. Why is it monoprotic?
options: The four hydrogens ionise together as one unit, counted as one proton
Only the hydrogen bonded to oxygen in the carboxyl group can ionise
Only the three hydrogens bonded to carbon are able to ionise in water
It is a weak acid, so it can only ever donate one of its four protons
questions.explanation: The O-H bond is polar and the ethanoate ion formed is stabilised, so this hydrogen is donated. The C-H hydrogens are not acidic in water. Being weak describes how much of the acid ionises, not how many protons each molecule can donate.

questions.stem: For phosphoric acid, the acidity constants for successive ionisations are in the order Ka1 > Ka2 > Ka3. Why?
options: Each proton is removed from an increasingly negative ion, which holds it more strongly
Each proton is removed from an increasingly positive ion, which repels it less strongly
Water molecules become less basic as more protons are donated to them by the acid
The later protons are bonded to phosphorus rather than to oxygen in the molecule
questions.explanation: H₃PO₄ is neutral, H₂PO₄⁻ carries a negative charge and HPO₄²⁻ carries two, so each further proton is attracted more strongly and is donated less readily. All three ionisable hydrogens are bonded to oxygen.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the second ionisation of carbonic acid in water?
options: H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
H₂CO₃(aq) + 2H₂O(l) ⇌ CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H₃O⁺(aq)
HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
questions.explanation: The first ionisation turns H₂CO₃ into HCO₃⁻, and the second removes a proton from HCO₃⁻ to give CO₃²⁻. Polyprotic acids ionise one step at a time, and the last equation shows HCO₃⁻ acting as a base.

questions.stem: What makes an acid strong?
options: It has more than one ionisable proton
It reacts with metals to produce hydrogen
It ionises completely in aqueous solution
It is present at a high concentration
questions.explanation: Strength describes the degree of ionisation. A strong acid donates essentially all of its protons to water. Concentration is a separate idea: a strong acid can be dilute, and a weak acid can be concentrated.

questions.stem: What is the acidity constant expression for hydrofluoric acid, HF(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + F⁻(aq)?
options: Ka = [H₃O⁺][F⁻] / ([HF][H₂O])
Ka = [HF] / ([H₃O⁺][F⁻])
Ka = [H₃O⁺] / [HF]
Ka = [H₃O⁺][F⁻] / [HF]
questions.explanation: Ka is the equilibrium constant for the ionisation of the acid. Water is the solvent, so its concentration is constant and is left out of the expression.

questions.stem: Three weak acids have these acidity constants: HA, Ka = 2 × 10⁻⁴; HB, Ka = 5 × 10⁻⁶; HC, Ka = 7 × 10⁻¹⁰. Which 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution has the lowest pH?
options: HA
HB
HC
They all have the same pH
questions.explanation: A larger Ka means a greater degree of ionisation, so more H₃O⁺ at the same concentration and a lower pH. Equal concentrations do not give equal pH values for acids of different strength.

questions.stem: A 1.0 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid solution is about 0.4% ionised. How does its pH compare with that of 0.0010 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid?
options: The ethanoic acid has the higher pH, because a weak acid always has a higher pH
The ethanoic acid has the lower pH, because its [H⁺] is about 0.004 mol L⁻¹
The hydrochloric acid has the lower pH, because it is a strong acid
Both have pH 3.0, because each contains 0.001 mol L⁻¹ of ionised acid
questions.explanation: 0.4% of 1.0 mol L⁻¹ gives [H⁺] ≈ 0.004 mol L⁻¹, pH about 2.4, while the hydrochloric acid has [H⁺] = 0.0010 mol L⁻¹, pH 3.0. The weak acid's high concentration outweighs its low degree of ionisation, showing that strength and concentration are different ideas.

questions.stem: A 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution of a weak monoprotic acid has [H₃O⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. What percentage of the acid molecules are ionised?
questions.explanation: Percentage ionised = (1.0 × 10⁻³ / 0.10) × 100 = 1.0%. The value 3.0 is the pH of the solution, not a percentage.

questions.stem: Which salt dissolves to give a basic solution?
options: Sodium chloride, NaCl
Potassium nitrate, KNO₃
Sodium ethanoate, CH₃COONa
Ammonium chloride, NH₄Cl
questions.explanation: Ethanoate is the conjugate base of a weak acid, so it accepts protons from water: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻. Ammonium chloride is acidic, and the ions in NaCl and KNO₃ do not react appreciably with water.

questions.stem: Which salt dissolves to give an acidic solution?
options: Ammonium nitrate, NH₄NO₃
Sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃
Potassium chloride, KCl
Potassium ethanoate, CH₃COOK
questions.explanation: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the weak base ammonia, so it donates protons to water and produces H₃O⁺. Carbonate and ethanoate salts are basic, and KCl is neutral.

questions.stem: Which equation explains why a solution of ammonium chloride is acidic?
options: NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq)
Cl⁻(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCl(aq) + OH⁻(aq)
questions.explanation: The ammonium ion donates a proton to water, forming hydronium ions. Chloride is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so it is too weak a base to react with water, and the other two equations do not produce H₃O⁺.

questions.stem: Solutions of sodium hydrogensulfate, NaHSO₄, and sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, are prepared. Which statement correctly describes them?
options: The NaHSO₄ solution is basic and the NaHCO₃ solution is acidic
Both solutions are neutral, because both are salts of sodium
The NaHSO₄ solution is acidic and the NaHCO₃ solution is basic
Both solutions are acidic, because both anions contain hydrogen
questions.explanation: Both anions are amphiprotic, but HSO₄⁻ is a fairly strong acid and mainly donates protons, making the solution acidic. HCO₃⁻ accepts protons more readily than it donates them, so its solution is mildly basic. Containing hydrogen does not make a species act as an acid.

questions.stem: Why is a solution of sodium nitrate, NaNO₃, neutral?
options: Na⁺ produces OH⁻ and NO₃⁻ produces H₃O⁺ equally
NaNO₃ is a strong electrolyte, so it ionises fully
Nitrate ions accept protons from water molecules
Neither Na⁺ nor NO₃⁻ reacts appreciably with water
questions.explanation: NO₃⁻ is the conjugate base of the strong acid HNO₃, so it is far too weak a base to accept protons from water, and Na⁺ does not react with water. Being a strong electrolyte says nothing about whether the solution is acidic or basic.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a buffer solution?
options: A solution of a strong acid and its conjugate base in equal amounts, at any pH
A solution that neutralises any amount of acid that is added to it
A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added
A solution that keeps its pH at exactly 7 whatever is added to it
questions.explanation: A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts, so it can react with small additions of H⁺ or OH⁻. Its pH depends on the pair used and need not be 7, and a large addition will overwhelm it.

questions.stem: Which pair of substances, dissolved together in water in similar amounts, forms a buffer?
options: Sodium hydroxide and sodium chloride
Nitric acid and potassium nitrate
Ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate
Hydrochloric acid and sodium chloride
questions.explanation: A buffer needs a weak acid and its conjugate base. Chloride and nitrate are the conjugate bases of strong acids, so they are too weak to react with added H⁺.

questions.stem: A buffer contains ethanoic acid and ethanoate ions: CH₃COOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). A few drops of hydrochloric acid are added. Why does the pH change very little?
options: Added H₃O⁺ reacts with CH₃COOH, shifting the equilibrium right, so [H₃O⁺] barely rises
Added Cl⁻ ions react with the CH₃COOH, so the extra H₃O⁺ ions are cancelled out
The water in the buffer dilutes the added H₃O⁺ to a concentration too low to matter
Added H₃O⁺ reacts with CH₃COO⁻, shifting the equilibrium left, so [H₃O⁺] barely rises
questions.explanation: The ethanoate ions act as a reservoir of base: they combine with the added H₃O⁺ to form ethanoic acid, so by Le Chatelier's principle the system shifts left and most of the added acid is removed. Ethanoic acid is the component that reacts with added base, not added acid.

questions.stem: A small amount of sodium hydroxide is added to a buffer of ammonium chloride and ammonia: NH₄⁺(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₃(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). What happens?
options: OH⁻ removes H₃O⁺, the equilibrium shifts right as NH₄⁺ ionises, and the pH rises only slightly
OH⁻ reacts with NH₃ to form NH₄⁺, the equilibrium shifts left, and the pH falls slightly
OH⁻ removes H₃O⁺, the equilibrium shifts left as NH₃ is used up, and the pH rises sharply
OH⁻ ions do not react with any species in this buffer, so its pH does not change at all
questions.explanation: The added hydroxide neutralises H₃O⁺. The system shifts right to replace it, converting NH₄⁺ into NH₃, so the pH rises only slightly. Hydroxide reacts with the acid component, NH₄⁺, not with ammonia.

questions.stem: Which of these ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate buffers has the greatest buffering capacity?
options: 0.10 mol L⁻¹ of each component
1.0 mol L⁻¹ acid, 0.010 mol L⁻¹ salt
0.010 mol L⁻¹ acid, 1.0 mol L⁻¹ salt
1.0 mol L⁻¹ of each component
questions.explanation: Buffering capacity is greatest when both components are present at high and similar concentrations, so there is plenty of weak acid to react with added base and plenty of conjugate base to react with added acid. A buffer with very little of one component is quickly used up in one direction.

questions.stem: Which conjugate pair is the main buffer system in human blood plasma?
options: Hydroxide ions and carbonate ions
Carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions
Hydrochloric acid and chloride ions
Phosphoric acid and phosphate ions
questions.explanation: Blood pH is kept near 7.4 mainly by the H₂CO₃/HCO₃⁻ pair. Hydrochloric acid is strong, so chloride is not a working base, and H₃PO₄ and PO₄³⁻ differ by three protons, so they are not a conjugate pair.

questions.stem: Pure water conducts electricity only very slightly. Why?
options: Its ions are held in a lattice by hydrogen bonds and cannot move
It ionises completely, but the ions it forms carry no charge
It self-ionises only to a tiny extent, so it has very few ions
It is a covalent molecule, so it can never form any ions at all
questions.explanation: Water is a weak electrolyte: 2H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) lies far to the left, so at 25 °C [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹. These few ions carry a very small current.

questions.stem: At 25 °C, a solution has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. What is [OH⁻]?
options: 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹
1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol L⁻¹
1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol L⁻¹
1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, so [OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 1.0 × 10⁻³ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹ mol L⁻¹. Only in a neutral solution are both 1.0 × 10⁻⁷.

questions.stem: At 50 °C, Kw = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴. Which statement about pure water at 50 °C is correct?
options: Its pH is above 7, so it is slightly basic
Its pH is exactly 7, because it is pure water
Its pH is below 7, but it is still neutral
Its pH is below 7, so it is slightly acidic
questions.explanation: A larger Kw means more self-ionisation, so [H⁺] is above 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ and the pH is about 6.6. Water stays neutral because [H⁺] still equals [OH⁻]. A pH of 7 marks neutrality only at 25 °C.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.025 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Nitric acid is strong, so [H⁺] = 0.025 mol L⁻¹ and pH = −log(0.025) = 1.60. The value 12.40 is what 14 − 1.60 gives, which would be the pH if 0.025 mol L⁻¹ were the hydroxide concentration.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.020 mol L⁻¹ barium hydroxide, Ba(OH)₂, solution at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: Each Ba(OH)₂ gives two OH⁻, so [OH⁻] = 0.040 mol L⁻¹ and [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ / 0.040 = 2.5 × 10⁻¹³ mol L⁻¹, giving pH 12.60. Forgetting the factor of two gives 12.30, and 1.40 is −log[OH⁻], not the pH.

questions.stem: A solution has a pH of 3.40. What is its hydrogen ion concentration?
options: 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹
2.5 × 10⁻¹¹ mol L⁻¹
4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹
3.4 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹
questions.explanation: Since pH = −log[H⁺], [H⁺] is 10 raised to the power −3.40, which is 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹. The value 2.5 × 10⁻¹¹ is the hydroxide ion concentration at 25 °C.

questions.stem: 20.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid is mixed with 15.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide at 25 °C. What is the pH of the mixture?
questions.explanation: n(H⁺) = 0.00200 mol and n(OH⁻) = 0.00150 mol, leaving 0.000500 mol H⁺ in 35.0 mL: [H⁺] = 0.0143 mol L⁻¹, pH 1.85. Dividing by 20.0 mL instead of the total volume gives 1.60.

questions.stem: 10.0 mL of a sodium hydroxide solution of pH 12.0 is diluted with water to 1.00 L at 25 °C. What is the pH of the diluted solution?
questions.explanation: [OH⁻] starts at 1.0 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ and is diluted 100-fold to 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹, so [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ and the pH is 10.0. Diluting a base lowers its pH towards 7; it cannot cross to an acidic pH such as 4.0.

questions.stem: What is an acid-base indicator?
options: A salt that reacts with H₃O⁺ ions to form a coloured precipitate in acid
A weak acid or weak base whose acidic and basic forms are different colours
A strong acid that changes colour when it is completely neutralised by a base
A substance that turns colourless at pH 7 and coloured at every other pH
questions.explanation: An indicator, HIn, is a weak acid in equilibrium with its conjugate base, In⁻. The two forms have different colours, so the colour shows which form predominates at that pH.

questions.stem: An indicator ionises as HIn(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ In⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq), where HIn is red and In⁻ is yellow. What colour is it in a strongly acidic solution, and why?
options: Red, because the high [H₃O⁺] shifts the equilibrium towards HIn
Yellow, because the high [H₃O⁺] shifts the equilibrium towards In⁻
Red, because the acid reacts with In⁻ to form a red precipitate
Yellow, because acid removes HIn by reacting with it to form water
questions.explanation: Adding H₃O⁺ increases the reverse rate, so by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts left and the red HIn form predominates. In a basic solution, OH⁻ removes H₃O⁺ and the yellow In⁻ form predominates.
